paragraphs: I've spent a long time watching West Walnut Creek, and fully renovated 1950s ranches on large lots don't come along often. When 2660 Ross Place hit the market this spring, the combination of a complete systems overhaul, dual master suites, and a 10,372-square-foot lot made it one of the more compelling offerings I'd seen at this price point in a while. When the listing came off market after 28 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out personally, because I think the home's story wasn't being told in a way that justified the number.

At $874 per square foot, this home sits at the upper end of the Walnut Creek premium tier, and that's a position that requires a specific kind of marketing support to hold. The listing description does mention the renovation, but it leads with category language like 'luxury real estate' and 'opulent bathrooms' rather than the concrete details that actually build buyer confidence at this price, things like the new electrical, new plumbing, and new HVAC that represent real, meaningful capital investment. Buyers comparing carefully online need those specifics spelled out. When they aren't, the price feels like an ask rather than a conclusion.

I've put together a short analysis of what I think the friction points were and how I'd approach the relaunch differently. It covers the pricing position relative to the Walnut Creek market, the visual and narrative gaps in how the home was presented, and a distribution strategy built for the buyers who are actively looking for exactly what this home offers.

If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside entirely. If you're not, I'd welcome a conversation, no pressure, just a look at the numbers together and a candid discussion about what a different approach might produce.

exec_summary.headline: A Fully Gut-Renovated West Walnut Creek Ranch on a 10,000-Square-Foot Lot  -  and a Listing That Didn't Build the Case for It
exec_summary.p1: 2660 Ross Place has the kind of substance that serious Lamorinda-adjacent buyers are actively searching for. A complete renovation means new electrical, new plumbing, new central HVAC, new flooring, and dual-pane windows throughout, not cosmetic updates, but a full systems rebuild inside a home with real bones. The 10,372-square-foot lot gives it outdoor scale that's genuinely rare at this price point in West Walnut Creek. The dual master suite layout addresses a specific and growing buyer need, particularly for multigenerational households or buyers who work from home and want separation. These are not generic selling points. They're the kind of specifics that move buyers from interest to offers.
exec_summary.p2: The listing came off the market after 28 days without a sale, and the gap between the home's actual investment and the outcome points to a strategy problem, not a property problem. At $874 per square foot, the listing sat at the upper end of the Walnut Creek premium tier. That position is defensible given the scope of renovation, but only if the marketing makes the case with precision. The description leaned on adjectives like 'opulent' and 'exquisite' without grounding them in the specifics that let buyers do the math. Buyers comparing options at this price point are sophisticated, and they needed more than mood language to justify the number.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to accomplish one clear thing: replace the adjective-heavy narrative with a concrete, evidence-based case for the price. That means leading with the capital investment the renovation represents, giving buyers the visual depth to understand the lot and the floor plan, and putting the listing in front of the specific buyer segments, Bay Area professionals, multigenerational families, and relocation buyers, who are most likely to see the value in what this home actually is.

forensics.title: Friction #1: A Premium Price Position Without the Supporting Evidence
forensics.body: At $874 per square foot, this home priced into the upper end of the Walnut Creek premium tier. That number is supportable, the full systems renovation alone represents significant capital, and the 10,372-square-foot lot adds real land value. But buyers comparing this home against others in the $1.3M to $1.5M range need to understand specifically why this one commands more per square foot than a standard updated home. The listing description used words like 'opulent' and 'luxury' without ever quantifying the renovation scope in terms buyers could verify and believe. When the marketing doesn't build that case, price-conscious buyers move on before they schedule a showing, and the number starts to feel unsupported.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork uses Zillow Showcase placement to present an evidence-based narrative directly on the listing page, one that spells out the renovation investment in concrete terms so buyers arrive at the showing already convinced, not skeptical.

forensics.title: Friction #2: A Visual Story That Was Never Told
forensics.body: A fully renovated home on a 10,000-plus-square-foot lot lives or dies on photography and spatial presentation. Buyers shopping at this price point are often doing significant research before they ever schedule a showing, and they need to be able to see what the renovation actually produced, the kitchen island, the dual master suite layouts, the lot dimensions and outdoor potential, in enough detail to feel something. Standard MLS angles rarely capture the open floor plan flow or the lot scale that make this property distinctive. If the photography didn't put buyers inside the experience, the listing description certainly didn't do it for them.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: A 3D Matterport tour lets buyers walk through the full floor plan from anywhere, at any time, giving out-of-area and busy professional buyers the spatial understanding they need to justify making the drive.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Right Buyers Were Never Actively Found
forensics.body: At $1,399,999 in the current rate environment, the buyer pool is selective by definition. The buyers most likely to respond to a fully renovated, large-lot West Walnut Creek home with dual master suites include Bay Area professionals relocating east of the tunnel, multigenerational families prioritizing layout flexibility, and buyers upgrading from smaller Contra Costa properties. These buyers don't materialize from passive MLS syndication alone. They need to be reached where they're already searching, which in 2026 means targeted digital channels built around the specific buyer profile, not a standard listing distribution and a wait.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork runs geo-targeted digital campaigns into San Francisco and Oakland buyer segments who are actively researching Walnut Creek before they've found what they're looking for, putting this home in front of decision-makers rather than browsers.

positioning_table.verdict: At $874/sqft versus a benchmark range of $820-$950/sqft, this home sits in the middle of that range. At $874 per square foot, this home sits in the upper portion of the Walnut Creek premium tier, and the full renovation scope genuinely supports that position. The lot size adds measurable land value that comparables on smaller parcels can't match. What the numbers needed was a marketing strategy that made this case explicitly and early, so buyers at this price point were building conviction rather than raising questions.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Building an Evidence-Based Case for the Price
pillars.body: The renovation at 2660 Ross Place was comprehensive: new electrical, new plumbing, new HVAC, new flooring, dual-pane windows throughout. That's a meaningful capital investment, not a cosmetic refresh, and it's the foundation of the $874-per-square-foot price position. A relaunch needs to lead with that investment in specific, quantifiable terms that buyers can verify. BrightWork builds listing narratives the way a great buyer's agent describes a home, grounded in evidence that arms buyers with the confidence to justify the number before they ever walk through the door.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Giving Buyers the Visual Depth to Understand This Home
pillars.body: The open floor plan, the dual master suite configuration, and the 10,372-square-foot lot are features that require the right presentation to land. Flat MLS photography rarely captures a floor plan's spatial logic or a lot's true scale. BrightWork's standard media package includes a Sky Tour that shows the lot position and street presence in context, giving buyers an understanding of what they're getting that satellite images and ground photography can't replicate. More informed buyers mean fewer wasted showings and more confident offers.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Reaching the Buyer Segments Most Likely to Act
pillars.body: The buyer for this home isn't browsing Zillow casually. They're a Bay Area professional who has decided to move east of the tunnel, a multigenerational family that needs layout flexibility, or a buyer upgrading from a smaller Contra Costa home who understands what a full renovation means. These buyers can be found and reached before they've narrowed their search to specific listings. BrightWork's geo-targeted campaigns are built around profiles like these, putting this home in front of the right people at the right stage of their decision, not after they've already committed elsewhere.
